en: The Essential Explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva,
with commentary by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of the West.

To begin with, the Buddhas, out of compassion for the deluded masses, bestow their transformative teachings according to individual capacities; though the return to the source is non-dual, the expedient means are manifold. Yet, among all these expedient means, none is as direct, swift, perfect, and sudden as the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

Furthermore, among all the Dharma-gates for the recollection of the Buddha, if one seeks that which is most simple and most reliable, nothing compares to single-mindedly upholding the Name with faith and aspiration. This is why, although the three Pure Land sutras circulate together in the world, the ancients singled out the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (the *Amitābha Sūtra*) as their daily practice. Is this not because they perceived that the single method of upholding the Name universally accommodates the three capacities of practitioners; it encompasses both phenomena and principle without omission and unifies both doctrine and practice without exception—is this not truly inconceivable!

Since antiquity, there have been no shortages of those who have provided commentaries and sub-commentaries; yet as time has passed, these works have largely fallen into obscurity, with but few remaining extant. Master Yunqi composed the *Sūchāo*, which is both vast and subtle; and the Venerable Master Youxi authored the *Yuánzhōngchāo*, which is lofty, profound, and expansive.

These are like the sun and moon in the midst of the sky, visible to all who possess eyes. However, because their texts are so voluminous and their meanings so manifold that their limits are unfathomable, beginners and those of shallow understanding may find it difficult to advance in their faith and aspiration. Therefore, I, disregarding my own mediocrity and folly, have once again set forth this Essential Explanation (*Yàojiě*). I do not dare to compete for originality with these two masters, nor do I dare to force myself to agree with them.

For example, when viewed from the side one sees peaks, and when viewed from the front one sees ridges; though neither perspective exhausts the true reality of Mount Lu, each nonetheless constitutes a direct personal vision of the mountain.
I shall now explain the fivefold profound meaning (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*) of the sūtra text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title: this sūtra is named after its speaker and the person spoken to.

As for "Buddha" (the Awakened One), he is the teaching master who speaks in this land, namely Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Riding upon the power of his vows of great compassion, he was born into this world of the five turbidities; having awakened first, he awakens those who awaken later. Because there is no dharma he does not know and no dharma he does not see, he is called a Buddha.

"To speak" means to express what one harbors in one's heart. The Buddha harbors the intent to deliver sentient beings; when the faculties of sentient beings have matured, the Buddha responds to the occasion by preaching the Dharma so that they may attain liberation, and thus he is "pleased."

Amitābha is the Teacher of that land as previously described; by means of his forty-eight vows, he receives those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha with faith and aspiration, causing them to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and forever attain the stage of non-retrogression.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called Amitābha; here [in Chinese], it is translated as "Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou) and also as "Immeasurable Light" (Wuliangguang).

To state the essentials: his merit and wisdom, his spiritual powers and divine strength, the adornments of his environment and his own body, and his preaching of the Dharma to transform and deliver beings—all these are immeasurable. For the sake of illustration, I have briefly cited two matters—his lifespan and his radiance—as the starting point for this discourse.

"Sūtra" (jīng) means instruction in the Dharma and instruction in the eternal; everything proclaimed from the golden mouth [of the Buddha] is generally termed a sūtra. Now, in contrast to the Buddha's teaching, the five characters for Amitābha constitute the title formed by combining both the general and the specific.
Regarding the three aspects of teaching, practice,
and principle, each has its own general and specific characteristics as extensively elucidated in the Tiantai Canon; one should seek these out for oneself, as they are not described here at length.
Second, regarding the discernment of the essence: all Mahāyāna sūtras take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their primary essence.
What is meant by the true mark?
It is precisely the intrinsic nature of the single thought-moment of the present.

The nature of the single thought-moment in our present experience does not abide within, nor without, nor in between; it is not of the past, nor the present, nor the future; it is not blue, yellow, red, or white; it is not long, short, square, or round; it is not fragrance, nor flavor, nor touch, nor dharmas. When sought, it is utterly ungraspable, yet one cannot say it is non-existent; it fully manifests the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, yet one cannot say it is existent. It is free from all marks of conceptualization and discrimination, yet conceptualization and discrimination do not possess a separate self-nature apart from this true reality. It is free from all marks of language and writing, yet language and writing do not possess a separate self-nature apart from this true reality.

To state it briefly: to be apart from all marks is to be identical with all dharmas. Because it is apart from all marks, it is markless; because it is identical with all dharmas, there is nothing that is not a mark. Since it is neither markless nor not markless, we have no choice but to provisionally name it "True Mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

The essence of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is neither quiescent nor illuminating; yet it is quiescent while constantly illuminating, and illuminating while constantly quiescent. It is metaphorically termed the "Land of Constant Quiescence and Light" because it is illuminating while constantly quiescent, and metaphorically termed the "Pure Dharma-body" because it is quiescent while constantly illuminating.
Furthermore, that which is luminous yet eternally quiescent is metaphorically termed the *dharmakāya*; that which is quiescent yet eternally luminous is metaphorically termed the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Moreover, the quiescence and illumination of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) are metaphorically termed the *dharmakāya*, while the quiescence and illumination of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) are termed the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Furthermore, the cultivation of virtue such that it is luminous yet eternally quiescent is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body); the cultivation of virtue such that it is quiescent yet eternally luminous is conventionally termed the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body).

One should know that quiescence and luminosity are non-dual, nature and cultivation are non-dual, and body and land are non-dual—all are nothing other than the true mark (*dharmatā*). This true mark is neither dual nor non-dual; therefore, its entire substance functions as the support, the principal, the dharma, the reward, the self, and the other. Even down to the speaker and the spoken, the savior and the saved, the believer and the believed, the aspirant and the aspiration, the upholder and the upheld, the progenitor and the progeny, and the praiser and the praised—none are not sealed by the seal of the true mark.
Third, the clarification of the school (zong): The school is the essential path for cultivation and the pivotal mechanism for realizing the essence;

it is the governing framework of all myriad practices. If one lifts the main cord, all the tassels will spread; if one grasps the collar, the sleeves follow accordingly. Therefore, following the clarification of the essence, one must next distinguish the school.
This sutra takes the practice of holding the Name through faith and aspiration as its essential core for cultivation.

Without faith, it is insufficient to arouse aspiration; without aspiration, it is insufficient to guide practice; and without the sublime practice of holding the Name, it is insufficient to fulfill one’s aspirations and realize what one has believed. Therefore, the sutra first expounds upon the Pure Land—the environment and its inhabitants—to engender faith; next, it exhorts one to generate aspiration to guide practice; and finally, it demonstrates how seven days of holding the Name lead directly to the stage of non-retrogression.

Faith consists of faith in oneself, faith in others, faith in causes, faith in effects, faith in phenomena, and faith in principle; aspiration consists of wearying of and detaching from the Sahā world while joyfully seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and practice consists of upholding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction.

Regarding "faith in oneself": one has faith that the single thought-moment of my present mind is fundamentally neither a physical lump of flesh nor a shadow dependent on conditions; vertically it is without beginning or end, and horizontally it transcends all boundaries, following conditions all day long yet remaining unchanging all day long.

The lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of empty space, are fundamentally things manifested within the single thought of my own mind. Although I am now deluded and confused, if I can for a moment turn my mind back toward it, I will certainly attain rebirth in the inherently present Land of Ultimate Bliss within my own heart; of this there is no doubt. This is called "believing in oneself."

"Faith in others" means having faith that Śākyamuni Tathāgata certainly has no deceptive speech, that Amitābha Bhagavat certainly has no empty vows, and that the broad and long tongues of the Buddhas of the six directions certainly have no double-tongued words; thus, one accords with the true instructions of all Buddhas, resolves to seek birth [in the Pure Land] without further doubt—this is called faith in others.

Regarding faith in the cause: one must have deep faith that even invoking the Name amidst distraction serves as the seed for attaining Buddhahood; how much more so, then, when the mind is single-minded and undisturbed—how could this not be the cause for birth in the Pure Land!
This is called faith in the cause. Regarding faith in the result:

one has deep faith that the gathering of superior virtues in the Pure Land all arises from the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like planting melon seeds and obtaining melons, or planting bean seeds and obtaining beans; it is also like a shadow necessarily following a form, or an echo necessarily responding to a sound. There is absolutely no such thing as a vain or wasted effort—this is called faith in the result.

Regarding the "matter of faith": because one has deep faith that the single thought-moment of the present is inexhaustible, one understands that all the worlds of the ten directions manifested by the mind are likewise inexhaustible. There truly exists the Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands, supremely pure and adorned, which is not like the metaphorical fictions of Zhuangzi; this is called the matter of faith.

Regarding the principle of faith: although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is situated a hundred trillion lands away, it truly does not lie outside this present, infinitesimal thought-moment of my own; for the nature of my present thought-moment has no external realm whatsoever.

Furthermore, one should have deep faith that all things in the Western Quarter—whether the environment and its inhabitants, or the principal and its retinue—are reflections manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind of my own present single thought-moment. Herein, phenomena are entirely identical to principle; delusion is entirely identical to truth; cultivation is entirely identical to nature; and the other is entirely identical to the self. Because my own mind is all-pervasive, the Buddha-mind is likewise all-pervasive; because the Buddha-mind is all-pervasive, the fundamental nature of the minds of all sentient beings is also all-pervasive.

It is like a single room illuminated by a thousand lamps, where each light pervades the others in mutual interpenetration; they are layered and mutually encompassing without any obstruction. This is called "believing in the principle.

Having attained such faith, one realizes that the Sahā world is the defilement manifested by one's own mind, and thus the principle of the mind's defilement dictates that one must feel weary of it and seek renunciation.

Conversely, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the purity manifested by one's own mind, and thus the principle of the mind's purity dictates that one should joyfully seek it. One must renounce defilement until, reaching the ultimate, there is nothing further to renounce; one must embrace purity until, reaching the ultimate, there is nothing further to grasp.
Therefore, the *Miaozongchao* states:
"If one’s engagement in acceptance and rejection reaches its extreme, this is not a different path from non-acceptance and non-rejection.

Now, if one does not engage in acceptance and rejection but merely prizes non-acceptance and non-rejection, this is to cling to principle while abandoning phenomena; since phenomena are abandoned, the principle is likewise not perfect."

If one realizes that the entirety of phenomena is itself the principle (li), then both taking up and relinquishing are themselves the principle; whether one takes up or relinquishes, there is nothing that is not the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Therefore, following faith, the aspiration (praṇidhāna) is elucidated.

Regarding the phrase "holding the name with single-mindedness and without confusion," the name is used to summon virtue; since that virtue is inconceivable, the name and its merit are likewise inconceivable. Because the merit of the name is inconceivable, even calling it out in a distracted state constitutes the seed of Buddhahood—how much more so for one who holds it with single-mindedness and without confusion? Who, then, would not ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression?

However, the essential practices for the Pure Land shown in various sutras differ in myriad ways and thousands of variations—such as visualizing images, contemplating the mind, prostrating, making offerings, performing the five repentances, and the six recollections—and the successful accomplishment of each of these practices leads to rebirth in the Pure Land.

Yet, among them, this single method of holding the Name gathers the widest range of capacities and is the easiest to undertake. Therefore, the Compassionate Honored One Śākyamuni, within this sutra, spoke of it spontaneously without being asked, specifically highlighting it before the Great Wisdom Śāriputra. It may be called the foremost of all skillful means, the unsurpassed ultimate meaning among all definitive teachings, and the most perfectly sudden and complete among all round and immediate methods.
Therefore, an ancient said:
"When a bright pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot help but become clear;
when the name of the Buddha is cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot help but become Buddha."

Taking faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name as the true cause of the One Vehicle, and taking the four kinds of Pure Lands as the wondrous fruit of the One Vehicle—since the fruit must necessarily follow when the cause is raised—the holding of the Name with faith and aspiration is established as the main body of the Sūtra.

As for the characteristics of the four kinds of pure lands, they are detailed in the *Miaozongchao* and the *Fannwang Xuanyi*; I shall not describe them here in full, but leave them for later commentary based on the main texts, where I will provide a brief indication.
The fourth section clarifies the power and function: rebirth without regression constitutes the power and function.
There are four lands for rebirth, each of which may be discussed in terms of the nine grades; for now, I shall briefly clarify the characteristics of attaining rebirth in these four lands.

If one upholds the Name but has not yet severed the afflictions of views and thoughts, then according to whether their state is distracted or concentrated, they are divided into three grades and nine ranks within the Land of Common Residence itself.

If one maintains the name until reaching the stage of "single-mindedness without distraction" (*shixin buluan*) and the delusions of views and thoughts (*jianxi*) fall away spontaneously first, then one will be born in the Pure Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*fangbian youyu jingtu*).

If one upholds the name until reaching the principle of single-mindedness without distraction, and thereby shatters from one to forty-one grades of ignorance, one will be born in the Pure Land of True Reward Adornment; this is also called the land of partial realization of the eternal light of stillness.
If ignorance is completely severed and exhausted, this is the supreme true recompense, which is also the ultimate land of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā*).
There are four meanings of non-retrogression:
first, non-retrogression in thought;
2. Non-retrogression in practice;
3. Non-retrogression in stage;
4. Ultimate non-retrogression.

First, those who do not regress in mindfulness break through the unmanifest and reveal their Buddha-nature, proceeding directly to the stage of actual retribution where they partially realize the Land of Quiescent Light.

Second, those who do not regress in practice have already cast off the afflictions of views and thoughts and further shattered the dust-like delusions; they are born in the Land of Expedient Means and advance toward the ultimate fruit.

Third, regarding non-retrogression in rank: those who are born into the Land of Common Residence while still carrying their karmic burdens will rest upon the substance of a lotus flower, forever free from conditions for retrogression.

Fourth, regarding ultimate non-retrogression: regardless of whether one’s mind is focused or distracted, conscious or unconscious, understanding or ignorant—if the Name of Amitābha Buddha passes once through the faculty of hearing, or if the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the title of this very sutra, pass once through the ear, then even after ten million kalpas, one will ultimately be delivered by virtue of this. It is like hearing the "poisoned drum," where both those near and far perish; it is also like eating a small piece of *vajra*, which is certain never to be digested.

Regarding the fifth aspect of the teaching: this is subsumed within the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Piṭaka; it is a self-proclaimed discourse delivered without being requested; it is sustained by the empowerment of ultimate great compassion; and it enables sentient beings of the final age, who face many obstacles, to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression by relying upon it.

Therefore, even after the extinction of the other sutras and teachings, this sutra remains in the world for a hundred years through the power of compassionate resolve, extensively delivering all sentient beings.
It is like the Agada medicine that holds mastery over all maladies; it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable.

The profound treasury of the *Avataṃsaka* and the secret marrow of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the essential heart of all Buddhas and the compass for the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas—all are contained herein and do not transcend this.
Should one wish to praise and describe it in detail, even an entire kalpa would not suffice; those with wisdom shall understand this for themselves.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the introduction (nidāna); second, the main body (śarīra); and third, the dissemination (pariṇāmanā).
These three divisions are called "good in the beginning," "good in the middle," and "good in the end"; it is not permissible for even one to be missing.
The introductory section (nidāna) is like the head of a person, wherein the five sense organs are fully present.
The "Correct Teaching" (Zhengzong) is like the human body, with its internal organs complete and without deficiency.
The "Circulation Section" (Liutongfen) is like the hands and feet, whose movement is unhindered.

Therefore, when the Great Master Zhiyi commented on the *Lotus Sūtra*, he designated the first chapter as the introduction, the middle fifteen and a half chapters as the correct teaching, and the final eleven and a half chapters as the circulation section.

Furthermore, at another time, the two gates—the Trace and the Source—were each divided into three sections; thus, from the "Dharma Master" chapter through the five chapters on "Peaceful Practices," all constitute the circulation section of the Trace Gate.

In essence, a preface must provide a comprehensive overview of the sutra’s structural framework, whereas circulation ensures that this Dharma-gift does not remain obstructed in future generations; thus, their significance is by no means trivial.

Later generations, failing to understand this, would see any passage in the sutra text that slightly touched upon doctrinal principles and categorically judge it to belong to the "True Teaching" (zhengzong). Consequently, they reduced the Prologue and the Dissemination sections to being no more than a three-inch hat or a pair of straw sandals—how could such a view possibly claim that "the words at the beginning are good, the words in the middle are good, and the words at the end are also good"?
First, the introductory section (nidāna), which has two parts:
first, the general introduction;
second, the specific introduction.
The first part consists of two sections:
first, the designation of the time and place of the Dharma assembly;
second, the invitation of the great assembly to hear it together.
Now, first: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Thus, "thus" (evam) indicates faith and compliance; "I heard" (śrutam) indicates the lineage of the teacher; "at one time" (ekasmin samaye) indicates the resonance between the capacity of the disciples and the response of the teacher; "the Buddha" (buddhaḥ) indicates the Master who teaches; and "Śrāvastī, the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park" indicates the location where the sutra was preached.

In this way, the wondrous principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) remains unchanging through all time, past and present, and is thus called "Suchness" (tathatā). To contemplate the Buddha based on this principle of the true mark and seek birth in the Pure Land with certainty and without error is called "Is-ness" (iti).

I, Ānanda, who am the hearer, thoroughly understand the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*): it is neither "self" nor "non-self. Because conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are not destroyed, I am still called "I.
When the faculty of hearing gives rise to the auditory consciousness to personally listen to the perfect sound, it is like space sealing space; therefore, it is called "hearing."

"Once upon a time" (*ekasmin samaye*): Time has no substantial reality; it is merely designated as "once" because the teacher and disciples were in perfect accord, and the assembly’s discourse and listening were fully completed from beginning to end.
"Buddha": He is self-awakened, awakened others, and perfected in the practice of awakening; as the Great Teacher of humans and devas, he is called Buddha.
Śrāvastī, here translated as "Hearing Things," is the name of a great kingdom in Central India, where King Prasenajit resided.
As for Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma: the prince of King Prasenajit was named Jeta, which here means "Victorious in Battle."

The minister of King Bimbisāra was the elder named Sudatta, which translates as "Giver of Orphans" (Jigudu). When the Elder Sudatta spread gold to purchase a grove for the Buddha and the Sangha, there remained a small portion of land that had not yet been covered. Jeta, moved by admiration, refused to accept further payment and offered this remaining land as a gift; therefore, both names are preserved.
2. Listing the Great Assembly who Heard Together.
Three parts:
first, the assembly of śrāvakas; [the other two follow].
Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas;
third, the assembly of devas and humans.
The śrāvakas occupy the first place because, firstly, they possess the characteristics of those who have transcended the world.
Second, because [the Buddha] is constantly followed by them;
third, because the Buddha-dharma relies upon the Saṃgha for its transmission.
As for the Bodhisattva assembly being situated in the middle, it is because their physical marks are not fixed.
Second, because they do not follow constantly;
third, because they symbolize the meaning of the Middle Way.
As for the placement of the assembly of devas and humans at the end: first, because this is the characteristic of the mundane world.
Second, because ordinary beings and sages are intermingled;
third, to clarify that it is the natural order of things for external protectors and attendants to be present.
Regarding the first, the assembly of śrāvakas, there are again three [points]:
First, clarifying the categories and indicating their number;
second, defining their positions and extolling their virtues;
third, listing the names of the leaders.
Now, first:
“He was together with a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The word “together” (yǔ) carries the meaning of being in company.
A "great bhikṣu" is one who has received full ordination and has left the household life.
"Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term that is not translated because it contains three meanings:

first, the meaning of "mendicant" (bhikṣu), which means that with a single alms-bowl for sustenance, one possesses nothing in store and focuses exclusively on seeking the essential way out of suffering.
Second, the meaning of destroying evil: this refers to using right wisdom to observe so as to destroy the evil of afflictions, thereby not falling into attachment or views.

Third, the meaning of terrifying Māra: this refers to the fact that when one generates the aspiration for enlightenment and receives the precepts through the completion of the *karmavācanā*, Māra is immediately terrified.
"Seng" (Saṃgha), when fully expressed, is *saṃgha*; this translates as "harmonious assembly. In principle, harmony means collectively realizing unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).
In practice, there are six kinds of harmony: namely, harmony of body in dwelling together;

harmony of speech in being free from contention; harmony of mind in mutual joy; harmony of view in shared understanding; harmony of precepts in joint cultivation; and harmony of material goods in equal distribution.
Regarding the one thousand two hundred and fifty people: the three Kāśyapa brothers, along with their disciples and teachers, numbered one thousand;
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, along with their disciples and teachers, numbered two hundred;

and Yaśas, the son of a householder, and others numbered fifty. All of them were the first to attain liberation not long after the Buddha’s enlightenment; because they were moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, they became his constant retinue.
2. Second, the designation of rank and the praise of virtues:
"They are all great arhats, renowned to the world.
"Great arhats" indicates their rank; "renowned to the world" praises their virtues.
The term "Arhat" contains three meanings:
first, the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings," which is the fruit of the mendicant;
second, the meaning of "Slayer of Thieves," which is the fruit of destroying evil.
Third, the meaning of non-arising is precisely the fruit of terrifying Māra.

Furthermore, there are three distinct types of liberation: liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*), liberation through both [wisdom and concentration] (*ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukti*), and liberation without doubt (*akopya-vimukti*). Since this refers to liberation without doubt, it is called "Great."
Furthermore, he is in truth a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body who manifests as a śrāvaka to realize this inconceivable dharma of the Pure Land; therefore, he is called "Great.
Because he turns the wheel of the Buddha's teachings to extensively benefit humans and devas, he is widely known by all.
3. Listing the Names of the Foremost Disciples:

"The Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, Kālodāyin, Mahākaśyapa, Bakula, and Aniruddha."
These and other great disciples were called "Elders" (*sthavira*) because they were both venerable in virtue and seniority.

Śāriputra is translated here as "Son of the Śāri Bird" (*Śārikāputra*), and also as "Son of the Body" (*Kāyaputra*). His mother’s body was upright and her eyes were like those of the śārikā bird; he received his name from his mother. Among the assembly of *śrāvakas*, he was foremost in wisdom.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana—translated here as Dà Cǎishǔshì—is foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Mahākāśyapa—translated here as Dà Yǐnguāng—possessed a golden radiance upon his body; he was foremost in the superior practice of *dhūta* (ascetic purification) and, having received the Buddha’s mind-seal, became the first patriarch in the Western Land.
Mahākātyāyana—here translated as "Great Ornament"—was of the Brahmin caste from South India and was foremost in debate.
Mahākauṣṭhila—here translated as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra and was foremost in answering questions.
Revata, translated here as "Constellation," was foremost in being free from confusion and error.

Cūḍapanthaka, translated here as "Successor of the Path," attained awakening through the practice of breath-regulation due to his dull faculties; he could enter meditative absorption while reciting a single verse with inexhaustible eloquence, and was thus foremost in retaining the meaning of the teachings.
Nanda, here translated as "Joy," was the Buddha’s own younger brother; his physical appearance was foremost.
Ānanda, here translated as "Rejoicing," was the Buddha’s first cousin; he served as the attendant and was foremost in extensive learning.
Rāhula, here translated as "Obstructing," was the Buddha’s crown prince and foremost in secret conduct.
Gavāmpati, here translated as "Rumination," experienced this residual retribution for the suffering he endured in previous lives, and was foremost in receiving celestial offerings.

Pindola, translated here as "Immovable," is the name of the Venerable; Phalada, translated here as "Sharp Faculties," is the clan name of the Venerable. Having long dwelt in the world to receive offerings during the final age, he is the foremost field of merit.
Kālodāyin—translated here as "Black Light"—was the Buddha’s messenger and foremost in converting others.
Mahākaśyapa—translated here as "Lunar Mansion"—was foremost in his knowledge of the stars and constellations.
Bakkula—here translated as "Good Appearance"—was foremost in longevity.

Anuruddha, also called Aniruddha, is translated as "Free from Poverty," "Unextinguished," or "As One Wishes"; he was also the Buddha’s younger cousin and was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The phrase "these and other great disciples" serves as a summary to indicate those not explicitly named.

These great disciples were originally Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body who manifested as Śrāvakas to serve as a retinue of influence and response. Now, by hearing together in this assembly the merits of the Pure Land’s reception of beings, they are able to obtain the benefit of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate teaching). Spontaneously increasing their Path and diminishing rebirth, they purify their own Buddha-lands; thus, they are also termed the "assembly of those whose capacities correspond to the teaching."
Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"Together with all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—
Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, Bodhisattva Ajita, Bodhisattva Gandhahasti, Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, and such great bodhisattvas as these."
The term "and" (bing) refers to the preceding assembly of śrāvakas.

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva—here translated as "one who accomplishes sentient beings through the mind of the Great Way"—is a designation for one who practices both compassion and wisdom simultaneously, benefiting both self and others.

Mañjuśrī—here translated as Miaojixiang (Auspicious Subtlety) and also as Miaode (Sublime Virtue)—is the foremost in wisdom among the assembly of Bodhisattvas. As the Buddha is the Dharma King, those Bodhisattvas who succeed to the family legacy of the Buddha are called "Dharma Princes. Were it not for his courageous and authentic wisdom, he would be unable to realize and understand this Dharma-gate of the Pure Land; therefore, he occupies the very first position.

Ajita, which in this language means "Invincible," is the name of Maitreya Bodhisattva. He shall descend to be born as a Buddha in a future age; currently, he dwells in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Since his primary task is precisely to ultimately adorn and purify a Buddha-land, he is listed next.
*Kandahati* (乾陀訶提) is translated here as "Unceasing," because one practices through vast eons without even a moment's pause.
"Ever-Exerting" refers to being free from weariness while benefiting oneself and others.
The phrase "together with such great bodhisattvas" follows the same pattern as the preceding examples.

These bodhisattvas of profound stages must also seek rebirth in the Pure Land, because only by not being separated from seeing the Buddha, not being separated from hearing the Dharma, and not being separated from attending upon and making offerings to the Sangha can they swiftly and completely fulfill Bodhi.
Third, the assembly of devas and humans:
"Together with Śakra-devānām-indra and an immeasurable multitude of other devas.
The word "together with" (及) also refers to the aforementioned śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Śakra-devānām-indra is here called "the Able Lord"; he is the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the ruler of the four continents.

The term "etc. refers to those below him, such as the Four Heavenly Kings, and those above him, such as Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and even the realms of Form and Formlessness; hence, they are called "immeasurable devas."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the great assembly together," it means that the eight classes of beings, asuras, humans, non-humans, and so forth, were all present; there was not one among them who was not a practitioner capable of being subsumed within the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
The general introduction is concluded.
Second is the specific introduction, which is the introductory section on the occasion of the teaching.

Since the wondrous gateway to the Pure Land is exceedingly profound and inconceivable, such that no one could pose a question regarding it, the Buddha himself proclaimed the names of the environment and its inhabitants of that land to serve as the occasion for the teaching.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities of beings without error; seeing that this great assembly would obtain four benefits by hearing the wondrous gateway to the Pure Land, he did not wait for others to inquire, but spontaneously initiated the teaching himself, as in the lower fascicle of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, where he proclaims his own title, saying: "I am now Vairocana," and so forth.
The Great Master Zhiyi also classified this as the "Introductory Section on the Occasion," which can be understood by analogy.
"At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:

'From here, passing through a hundred trillion buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. In that land there is a Buddha, titled Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.'"

"The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land universally encompasses the three faculties; it is absolute, perfectly interfused, and inconceivable. Being profoundly deep and difficult to believe, he specifically calls upon those of great wisdom to speak with them, for it is not possible to immediately reach a state free of doubt without the foremost wisdom."
"From here" means from this Sahā world.
"The western direction" refers to the point directly westward, indicating the location where [the Buddha] manifests.
"Passing beyond" means transcending.
Regarding "one hundred trillion": ten million is called a *yì*; now, these *yì* are further accumulated up to one hundred thousand.

As for a "Buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*), the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system is collectively considered the realm transformed by a single Buddha, and is thus named a single Buddha-field.

To speak of this world-system: on each of the four sides—east, south, west, and north—of a single Mount Sumeru, there is one continent, all illuminated by the same sun and moon and surrounded by the same minor Cakravāḍa mountain range; this is called a single "four-continent system" (cāturdvīpaka).
One thousand such four-continent systems constitute a small chiliocosm.
One thousand small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm, which contains one million Mount Sumerus, four continents, suns, moons, and minor Cakravāḍa mountains.
A thousand times a thousand worlds is called a "great trichiliocosm," which contains one hundred thousand Mount Sumerus; therefore, it is named the "trichiliocosm of three thousandfold worlds.
Passing beyond such buddha-fields to the west for a total of ten trillion worlds, there lies the world of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
Question:
"For what reason is the Land of Ultimate Bliss definitely located in the west? Answer:
"This is not a good question. Even if Sukhāvatī were in the east, you would still have to ask why it is in the east;
would that not be mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*)?"
Moreover, when viewed from this Sahā world, Sukhāvatī lies to the west; yet if viewed from eleven trillion Buddha-lands away, Sukhāvatī would again lie to the east—so why should one harbor any doubt?
"There is a world named Sukhāvatī" introduces the name of the land as the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment resulting from karmic fruition).

"World" (*loka*) refers to the temporal flow of the past, present, and future; "world-system" (*dhātu*) refers to the spatial directions of east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below. Since this indicates the environment resulting from karmic fruition, it must necessarily be defined vertically by the three periods of time to distinguish its temporal kalpas, and horizontally by the ten directions to determine its spatial boundaries; hence it is called a "world."

Regarding the term "Ultimate Bliss" (Jile): in Sanskrit it is *Sukhāvatī*, which is translated here as "Ultimate Bliss," and is also translated as "Peaceful Nurturing" (*Āśraya*), "Peaceful Joy" (*Ananda*), or "Pure Tranquility. It refers to the state of being eternally free from all suffering and the foremost in security and peace, as will be explained in detail in the following text.

However, there are four types of Buddha-lands, each distinguished by being either pure or defiled. These are the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages: where the five turbidities are heavy, it is defiled; where the five turbidities are light, it is pure.

In the land of skillful means with remainder, that which is entered by those who analyze emptiness through clumsy means is defiled; that which is entered by those who realize emptiness through skillful means is pure.

In the land of true recompense without obstruction, that which is entered by those who realize it through the sequential threefold contemplation is defiled; that which is entered by those who realize it through the single-mind threefold contemplation is pure.
In the land of eternal quiescent light, those who have attained partial realization perceive it as defiled, while those who have attained ultimate, complete realization perceive it as pure.
Here, the text specifically refers to the Pure Land of Shared Residence, which also horizontally encompasses the three aforementioned pure lands.
"In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha" introduces the name of the principal teacher as the primary retribution.

"Buddha" is a general term, while "Amitābha" is a specific name; in the Sanskrit language, Amitābha means "Immeasurable Life," "Immeasurable Light," and so forth, as will be explained in detail below.
The Buddha has three bodies, whose names vary in their singular or plural usage:
"Dharmakāya" used in the singular refers to the principle of reality realized;
"Sambhogakāya" used in the singular refers to the merit and wisdom that realize it.
The "single" aspect of the nirmāṇakāya refers to the manifested marks, signs, and physical forms.
The "double" aspect of the dharmakāya consists of:
first, the naturally pure dharmakāya; [and second, the dharmakāya of pure excellence].
Second, the immaculate and most sublime Dharmakāya.
Regarding the Saṃbhogakāya, there are two types:
first, the self-enjoyment Saṃbhogakāya; [second, the other-enjoyment Saṃbhogakāya].
2. The Enjoyment Body for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*). Regarding the multiple Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*):
first, the Transformation Body that manifests birth; and so forth.
Second, the manifested transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Furthermore, there are two types: first, the transformation body of the Buddha-realm;
second, the transformation body that conforms to various classes of beings.

Although one may distinguish between the single and the multiple, or the three bodies, in reality they are neither one nor three, yet they are three and one; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither concurrent nor separate—transcending all faults and negations, they are inconceivable.

The present mention of Amitābha Buddha specifically refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested within the Land of Common Residence; yet, this very body is simultaneously the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*). Therefore, those who hear his name will certainly attain non-retrogression.

The phrase "now preaching the Dharma" distinguishes this from the past, which has already ceased, and the future, which is not yet realized; it refers to one who is currently preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Therefore, one should make a vow to be reborn there to personally attend upon this preacher of the Dharma and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is a world where a Buddha currently resides; this is the section on encouraging faith.
The world is named Sukhāvatī; this is the section on encouraging aspiration.
The Buddha’s name is Amitābha; this is the section on encouraging the sublime practice of holding his name.
Furthermore, "Amitābha" refers to the Buddha;
"preaching the Dharma" refers to the Dharma;
and since there must be an audience for the preaching of the Dharma, it refers to the Sangha.
The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha share the same true reality; this constitutes the "Preface" to the essence.
From this, one gives rise to faith, aspiration, and practice; this constitutes the "Preface" to the school.
When faith, aspiration, and practice are perfected, one will necessarily attain rebirth, see the Buddha, and hear the Dharma; this constitutes the "Preface" to the function.
The unique Buddha-realm alone serves as the object of focus, unmixed with any other matters; this constitutes the introductory section of the teaching.
The text is concise, yet its meaning is comprehensive.
The initial introductory section is concluded.
II. The Main Body (Zhengzongfen), in two parts:
First, a detailed exposition of the wondrous fruits of the environment and inhabitants of that land to inspire faith;
second, the formal exhortation for sentient beings to make vows and uphold the Name to establish the cause.

Faith and aspiration in the recitation of the Name are the essential purport of this sutra. Faith and aspiration constitute the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), while the recitation of the Name constitutes the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*). Whether one attains birth [in the Pure Land] or not depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and aspiration; whether one’s rank is high or low depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of the recitation. Thus, the practice of wisdom serves as the precursor, while the practice of conduct is the primary cultivation—like the simultaneous movement of the eyes and the feet.
The initial passage is divided into two parts:
first, the excellence of the land as the environment;
second, the excellence of the principal figures and their retinues as the primary retribution.
The first section also has two parts:
first, a general presentation of the names and meanings;
second, a detailed explanation of the adornments.
Now, first:
"Śāriputra! For what reason is that land named 'Supreme Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)?"
"The sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys; therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī).
In the Sahā world, suffering and joy are intermingled: suffering is the suffering of suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) because it oppresses both body and mind;
joy is the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā) because it does not endure for long."
Neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), because its nature is one of constant flux.

That land is eternally free from these three types of suffering; it does not consist of the "pleasures" that merely counteract suffering as they do in this land, and for this reason it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*).

In general, because the five turbidities are light in the Pure Land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, there is no suffering of the eight afflictions associated with the分段 (fen-duan) [limited] existence; rather, one experiences joys such as being free from illness and death, traveling at will, partaking of celestial food and wearing celestial garments, and gathering with those of supreme goodness.

In the Pure Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, because the essence of contemplation is so skillful, there is no suffering of sinking into emptiness or stagnating in quiescence; one experiences only the bliss of sporting with supernatural powers and the like.

In the Pure Land adorned by the true recompense, one realizes perfect enlightenment with a single mind; thus, there is no suffering of separation or lack of fusion, but only the experience of unimpeded, inconceivable bliss.

The Land of Tranquil Light is ultimately equal; therefore, it is free from the suffering of the Dharma-body’s seepage and the constant flow of the True-Constant, experiencing only the perfect, ultimate bliss that accords with the nature of reality.
II. Detailed Explanation of the Adornments, in four parts:
First, explaining the adornment of the ground and trees;
second, explaining the adornment of the colors of the ponds, towers, and flowers.
3. The adornment of the rain of flowers from the celestial music;
4. The adornment of the sound of the Dharma. First, [the explanation of the first].

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss, there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the four precious substances, surrounding it on every side; for this reason, that land is named Ultimate Bliss."
The railings adorn the boundaries, the nets adorn the space above, and the rows of trees adorn the open ground.
Each is said to be sevenfold to symbolize the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
The fact that they are all made of the four treasures symbolizes the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

As for "surrounded on all sides," it means that the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas in that land are immeasurable in number; thus there are immeasurable dwelling places, and there are also immeasurable sevenfold railings, jeweled nets, and rows of trees filling that land. Since the adornments everywhere are inexhaustible, it is said that they "surround it on all sides."

These adornments of the co-residing pure land are the result of superior wholesome karma and are also the result of the perfected five grades of contemplation; they take as their substance the subtle five sensory objects produced through dependent origination.

These adornments of the expedient pure land are produced by the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness itself, and they are also produced by the three contemplations in their semblance; they take as their substance the five sense objects of the untainted, wondrous ultimate truth.

The adornments of such a land of true retribution are produced by the wisdom of the wondrous provisional contemplation (*miào jiǎ guān*) and are also produced by the partial realization of the three contemplations; they take as their substance the inexhaustible five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the wondrous conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The adornments of the eternally quiescent light-realm (sadaśāntaprakāśadhātu) are thus produced by the wisdom of the Middle Way (madhyamaka), and are also produced by the ultimate threefold contemplation (trivipaśyanā); they take as their essence the five sensory objects (pañcaviṣaya) that accord with the nature of the wondrous Middle Truth (madhyamasatya).

To facilitate understanding, I have made this analysis; yet, if one grasps the underlying meaning, one will see that the adornments of the four lands are, one by one, nothing other than phenomena produced through causes and conditions, and that each and every one of them is none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
The following sections are all modeled after this; they will not be described in further detail.
Question:

"Regarding the three lands—the Land of Common Dwelling, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Real Retribution—it can be said that they possess all adornments such as railings, rows of trees, ponds, towers, and rains of flowers. Since the Land of Constant Quiescent Light consists solely of the principle of nature (li-xing), how can it also possess such adornments?"

Answer: "Each and every adornment is none other than the entirety of the rational nature; each and every rational nature is fully endowed with immeasurable adornments—only then is this the ultimate fruit of reliance of all Buddhas."

If it is claimed that the Land of Tranquil Light does not possess the five exquisite sensory objects, how does it differ from the partial truth of the Dharma-nature realized by the followers of the Lesser Vehicle?
Second, the description of the adornments of the ponds, towers, and flowers.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities. The bottoms of these ponds are entirely covered with golden sand, and their four-sided stairways and walkways are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Above them are multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, red pearls, and agate."

The lotuses in the pond are as large as chariot wheels; those that are blue emit a blue light, those that are yellow emit a yellow light, those that are red emit a red light, and those that are white emit a white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
"Śāriputra! The land of Ultimate Bliss is thus adorned with such meritorious qualities.
As for the 'pools of the seven treasures,' these are pools formed of the seven treasures, such as gold and silver, and are not composed of earth and stone like those of this world."

The eight qualities are: first, limpidity; second, coolness; third, sweetness; fourth, lightness; fifth, softness; sixth, purity; seventh, freedom from stench; eighth, the ability to nourish the body. First is limpidity; second is coolness.
Third, sweet; fourth, light and soft;
fifth, moist and lustrous.
Sixth, tranquility;
seventh, the removal of hunger and thirst;
eighth, the nourishment of the sense faculties.
That which fills its interior is not like this region, where at times it dries up and at times it overflows.
That the bottom of the pond is entirely covered with golden sand is unlike this region, where there is only foul mud.
The stairways by the ponds, composed of the four jewels, differ from those in this land, which consist merely of bricks and stone.

"Tier" (bì) refers to steps; "pathway" (dào) refers to a level road; "pavilion" (lóu) refers to a multi-storied building; and "tower" (gé) refers to a high, peaked structure. These too are adorned with the seven treasures, differing from those in this land, which consist merely of wood, earth, vermilion, and green.
Regarding the lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels: the golden wheel of a Cakravartin King is forty *li* in diameter; this refers merely to the smallest variety of flowers.
According to the *Contemplation Sūtra* and the "Infinite Life Chapter" of the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, however, the various sizes and categories of these flowers are truly immeasurable.
The blue is named *utpala*, the yellow is named *kumuda*, the red is named *padma*, and the white is named *puṇḍarīka*.
These flowers necessarily possess radiance, which is brought about by the influence of pure karma; they differ from the flowers of this region, which have color but lack radiance.
Furthermore, the light and color of the lotus flowers in Sukhāvatī are immeasurable; this sutra speaks of them only briefly.
The phrase "subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure" is a concise praise of the four virtues of the lotus flowers.

The concluding statement, "accomplishing such adornments of merit," clarifies that the various adornments described above are all accomplished through the merits of Amitābha Buddha’s great vows and great practices that accord with his true nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, they are able to universally adorn the four kinds of pure lands and universally gather all ordinary beings and sages of the ten directions and three periods of time, causing them to be reborn there.
Third, the adornment of the rain of heavenly music and flowers.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In that buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays, and the ground is made of gold. Six times throughout the day and night, it rains *māndārava* flowers. The sentient beings of that land always at dawn each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in other directions; then, at the time of eating, they return to their own land to eat and walk in meditation."
"Śāriputra! The land of Sukhāvatī is thus adorned with such meritorious qualities.
Because the subtle and exquisite musical sounds produced by the devas are constant and uninterrupted, it is said that "celestial music is constantly played."
The pure ground realm, adorned with the seven treasures, has gold as its substance; therefore, it is said that "the earth is made of gold.

The first part of the day and the latter part of the day are called the three periods of the day; the first part of the night, the middle part of the night, and the latter part of the night are called the three periods of the night; thus, it is said there are "six periods of day and night."

However, since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in that land each possess bodily radiance, and those beings who are born there likewise possess bodily radiance, they are always luminous and never dark; without relying on the light of the sun and moon, how are day and night distinguished?
Alternatively, they may take the blooming of flowers and the singing of birds as day, and the closing of flowers and the roosting of birds as night.
Or, although in reality there is no day or night, they provisionally employ the conventional designations of "day" and "night" in accordance with the habitual usage of this region.
*Mandāra* is the name for a celestial flower; here it is translated as "that which satisfies the mind" (*shiyi*) or "white flower.
Because it descends from the sky, it is called "rain.
"Sentient beings" refers to those from the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) above down to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) below.
A *kuci* (衣裓) is a vessel for holding flowers.

"Various wonderful flowers" refers to the celestial flowers that were rained down; this clarifies that they did not consist solely of the *māndārava* variety. They should be understood as the four types of flowers described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which symbolize the four stages of causal development: abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), orientation (*pratipatti*), and the grounds (*bhūmi*).
Making offerings to the Buddhas of other directions signifies that the true cause inevitably tends toward the ultimate fruit, and that the virtues of that fruit are all-pervasive.

The mention of "only ten million billion" refers to the fact that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is separated from this Sahā world by ten million billion lands; the intent is to show that once one has attained rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is not difficult to return and make offerings to Śākyamuni and Maitreya.
If one considers the empowerment bestowed by Amitābha’s supernatural power, how could there be any place he cannot reach?
That they return to their own land at the very time of a meal clarifies that his supernormal powers are sovereign and require no lapse of time.

Regarding "the practitioner who eats while walking": since it is said that this occurs at the time of eating, it is called "eating. When one is mindful of food, the food arrives of its own accord without waiting for preparation or arrangement; when the meal is finished, the bowl departs spontaneously without the need for washing, wiping, or putting it away. Therefore, one simply walks upon the precious ground, practicing with effortless spontaneity.

If the bliss of the Land of Pure Bliss, where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, is already such as this, how much more so must the bliss be when one can, within that very land, horizontally transcend the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Ultimate Reality!

This also has two parts: first, a specific explanation of the two kinds of sounds of the Dharma; second, [the general explanation]. First: a specific explanation of the two kinds of sounds of the Dharma.
