2. Resolving Doubts through Inquiry and Explanation. First:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wonderful birds of diverse colors—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas. These birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, utter harmonious and elegant sounds; their voices eloquently expound the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas as these."
When the sentient beings in that land hear these sounds, they all recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Thus it is said that the various wondrous birds of manifold colors are both numerous and beautiful.
Furthermore, I shall describe what is cherished and admired here by way of comparison.
The śāri is the *śārika* (the blue jay), as well as the white crane, the peacock, and the parrot—these four species all exist in this land and are prized by all people.
The kalaviṅka—translated here as "Wondrous Voice"—possesses a voice that surpasses all other birds even before it has emerged from its shell; such a bird does not exist in this land.
The jīvañjīvaka, a single-bodied bird with two heads that distinguishes their respective karmic retributions yet shares them together, likewise does not exist in this land.

These two kinds exist in places such as the Snow Mountains in the western lands; however, none can be compared to the wondrous birds of Sukhāvatī, for they are mentioned only as being similar to them.

To say that they produce harmonious and elegant sounds during the six periods of day and night implies that in the Pure Land, birds do not roost at night; one should know that in reality there is no day or night, though "day" and "night" are used as provisional designations. This is because those born by transformation from lotus flowers have bodies that are naturally free from drowsiness and thus have no need for nocturnal sleep.
Regarding the "five faculties, five powers, and so forth," these refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
The fact that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power are not mentioned is merely due to an abbreviation in the text.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment pertain to all four teachings.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
first, the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
2. The foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
3. The foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
4. The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The four right efforts are:
first, to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen;
second, to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising.
Third, to cause unarisen wholesome dharmas to arise;
fourth, to cause already arisen wholesome dharmas to increase.
As for the four bases of psychic power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ):
1. The basis of psychic power consisting of desire;
2. the basis of psychic power consisting of effort;
3. the basis of psychic power consisting of mind;
Fourth, the basis of psychic power consisting of reflection.
As for the five faculties, they are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
To have faith in the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment is called the faculty of faith.
Diligently seeking the true path and all wholesome dharmas that assist the path without ceasing is called the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*);
maintaining mindfulness of the true path and all wholesome dharmas that assist the path without any other thoughts is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*);
gathering the mind within the true path and all wholesome dharmas that assist the path so that it is in accord and not distracted is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is defined as the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering, for the sake of the True Path and its various auxiliary wholesome dharmas.
Regarding the five powers (*pañcabala*):
when the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) increases, it is able to destroy doubt, destroy all false beliefs, and destroy the afflictions; this is called the power of faith (*śraddhābala*).

The growth of the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) breaks various forms of physical and mental indolence and accomplishes the great matters of transcendence; this is called the power of diligence (*vīryabala*).

The growth of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) breaks all erroneous thoughts and achieves all meritorious qualities of correct mindfulness regarding transcendence; this is the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*).

The growth of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) can break distracted thoughts and give rise to meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) concerning both phenomena and principle; this is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*).
When the faculty of wisdom increases, it is able to obstruct both the pervasive and specific afflictions and give rise to true outflow-free wisdom; this is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
As for the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), they are also called the seven limbs of awakening:

first, when wisdom contemplates all phenomena, it is well able to discern the true from the false and does not erroneously grasp at deceptive phenomena; this is called the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

2. When diligently practicing the various dharmas of the path, one is skillfully able to awaken to them and does not mistakenly engage in fruitless asceticism; with a mind constantly diligent and dwelling within the true Dharma, this is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*). 3.

If the mind attains the joy of the Dharma, one is skillfully able to awaken to the fact that this joy does not arise based on inverted dharmas; dwelling in joy while abiding in the true joy of the Dharma, this is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*). 4.

When severing the afflictions of various views, one is skillfully able to awaken to the removal of all falsehoods without damaging the true and genuine roots of goodness; this is called the awakening factor of relinquishment (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*).

5. When one relinquishes attachment to objects as they appear, being well able to discern that the relinquished objects are false and unreal and never recollecting them again, this is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). 6.

When one gives rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), being well able to discern that all concentrations are provisional and not giving rise to craving, views, or deluded thoughts, this is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

7. When one cultivates the supramundane path, being well able to discern so as to always maintain the balance of concentration and wisdom: if the mind sinks, one should mindfully employ the three awakening factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*) to arouse it; if the mind is agitated, one should mindfully employ the three awakening factors of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and concentration (*samādhi*) to sustain it. This harmonious moderation is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The eightfold noble path is also called the eightfold right path:
first, practicing untainted cultivation to clearly perceive the four truths is called right view;

second, employing an untainted mind to engage in contemplation, exertion, awakening, discernment, and deliberation in order to increase [wholesome qualities] and enter great nirvana is called right thought.

Third, by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one eliminates the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), subsumes all verbal actions within all right speech, and this is called right speech (*samyagvāc*).
Fourth, by means of untainted wisdom, one eliminates all bodily wrong actions and abides in pure right bodily action; this is called right action (*samyakkarmānta*).

Fifth, by means of untainted wisdom, one universally eliminates the five types of wrong livelihood within the three types of action and abides in pure right livelihood; this is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*). As for the five types of wrong livelihood:
1. To feign extraordinary and marvelous signs for the sake of gain and offerings;
2. To speak of one's own merits for the sake of gain and offerings;
3. To practice divination of auspicious and inauspicious omens and preach the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings.
Fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings, raising one's voice and manifesting an air of authority to inspire awe and reverence in others;
fifth, for the sake of gain and offerings, speaking of the offerings one has received to stir the hearts of people;
sixth, applying oneself with diligence through wisdom free from outflows (*anāsrava-prajñā*) to cultivate the path to *nirvāṇa*, which is called right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).
Seventh, mindfulness that is associated with untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) regarding the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment is called right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti);
eighth, entering meditative absorption associated with untainted wisdom is called right concentration (samyak-samādhi).
If these factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) are cultivated based on the four truths of arising and ceasing, they constitute the path-factors of the Tripitaka Teaching;
if cultivated based on the four truths of non-arising, they constitute the path-factors of the Shared Teaching;
if cultivated based on the four truths of the immeasurable, they constitute the path-factors of the Distinct Teaching.
If one practices in accordance with the unconditioned Four Noble Truths, this constitutes the path-factors (mārga-aṅga) of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya).

The path-factors of the Treasury Teachings (Tripitaka-yāna) are termed the "half-syllable" dharma-gate; since the defilements are light in the Pure Land, these need not necessarily be employed, though they may be used temporarily for those of inferior capacity whose seeds have first ripened.

The *dharmapada* (stages of the path) of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) is called the "initial gateway to the Mahāyāna," which all three vehicles (*triyāna*) receive in common; it is frequently taught in the Land of Common Dwelling (*tongju jingtu*).

The *dharmapada* of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) is called the "exclusive Dharma of the Bodhisattvas"; it is also frequently taught in both the Land of Common Dwelling and the Land of Expedient Means (*fangbian jingtu*).

The factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) are called the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma; those of sharp faculties should be able to hear them all within the four pure lands.

The concluding phrase "such dharmas as these" refers to the aforementioned foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), and so forth, as well as all other dharma-gates of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Although all the Buddha-dharmas are fully encompassed within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, because the capacities and conditions of sentient beings are unequal, there are various ways of opening and closing these categories, resulting in different names and meanings.

In brief, whatever one wishes to hear is expounded without exception; thus, it enables all who hear it to give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Furthermore, regarding the Three Jewels thus recollected, there are differences in their distinct characteristics, their single essence, and even the meanings and intentions of the four teachings, as extensively clarified in other sutras and treatises.
2. Investigation, Explanation, and Dispelling of Doubts:
"Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are actually born as a result of their karmic retribution for transgressions."
Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land there are no three evil realms of existence.
In that Buddha-land, even the name of the evil realms does not exist, let alone their actual presence.
All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, intended to cause the sounds of the Dharma to flow forth.
Fearing that there might be doubt as to how there can be various birds in what is a pure land, he now explains:
These are not born as a retribution for sin; rather, Amitābha has manifested these various birds in order to cause the sound of the Dharma to circulate.
Question:
"If it is said that even the names of the evil realms do not exist there, then are the white cranes, peacocks, and so forth not merely names for the realm of animals?"
The answer is:

"Since these are not produced as retribution for transgressions, each and every name expresses the ultimate merits of the Tathāgata—such as 'Ultimate White Crane' and 'Ultimate Peacock. As these are none other than beautiful designations for inherent virtues, how could they be called evil realms!"

Question: "The Buddha wishes for the sound of the Dharma to flow forth; it would be acceptable for him to manifest in whatever form is necessary to transform beings. Why must he specifically manifest as various birds? Answer:
“There are four reasons for the *siddhāntas*:
first, because ordinary beings take pleasure in these birds, he transforms them by conforming to their inclinations so that they may rejoice;
second, because even birds can preach the Dharma, he causes those who hear it to give rise to wholesome roots.”
Third, because the birds are able to preach the Dharma, one should not conceive thoughts of inferiority toward them, thereby counteracting the discriminating mind;

fourth, because the birds are emanations created by Amitābha and are no different from the Dharmakāya of Amitābha, they cause one to realize that the Dharmakāya is equal, lacking nothing and accomplishing all things.
2. Sound of Wind in the Trees.

"Śāriputra! In that buddha-land, when a gentle breeze blows, the various rows of jewel trees and the jeweled nets produce a subtle and wondrous sound, like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously."
"Those who hear these sounds will naturally give rise to the mind that recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, and recollects the Sangha.

The Dharma-sounds of the various birds are the voices of sentient beings manifested through transformation; the Dharma-sounds of the wind and trees are the voices of insentient things manifested through transformation. Sentient and insentient alike proclaim the wondrous Dharma; all are accomplished by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows and manifested by his knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). All are evoked by our own pure karma and transformed by consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra).

The Buddha-mind and the sentient-being mind act as mutual reflections and shadows for one another; like the light of many lamps, each pervades everywhere yet appears as one. The entire principle constitutes phenomena, and the entirety of phenomena is identical to the principle; the entire nature gives rise to cultivation, and the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature. Readers should likewise reflect upon this deeply and at length.
How can one abandon this Pure Land to discourse separately on "Mind-Only," thereby willingly subjecting oneself to the derision of being like a mouse that falls into a bird’s nest?
This concludes the initial separate elucidation of the two kinds of Dharma-sounds.
2. Conclusion: Praise of the Accomplishment of Merit. "Śāriputra!
That buddha-field is thus adorned with the accomplishment of such merits."
Thus, through repeated and profound praise, he seeks to cause those who hear it to have deep faith and no doubt.
First, the description of the excellence of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment or dependent retribution) of the land is concluded.
Second, the description of the excellence of the *vipāka-vipāka* (the primary retribution or the principal being) and their attendants, in two parts:
First, the excellence of the Teacher;
second, the excellence of the retinue.
Within the first, there are two parts:
First, a general inquiry;
second, a detailed explanation.
Now, the first [section].
“Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha?”
2. The detailed explanation has two parts:
first, the explanation in terms of light;
second, the explanation in terms of lifespan.
Now, first: "Śāriputra!
That Buddha’s radiance is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction. For this reason, he is named Amitābha."

Because the nature of the mind is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it is called "light. Now, having thoroughly realized the immeasurable essence of the nature of the mind, its light is immeasurable.

All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time have fully and thoroughly realized the entire body of the nature of the mind; they all illuminate the lands of the ten directions without obstruction, and all may be termed "Immeasurable Light. However, due to differences in the power of their vows during the causal stage, each has established a distinct name according to their respective causes and conditions.

In the past, when the Buddha was the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, he made forty-eight vows, among which was the vow that his radiance would constantly illuminate the ten directions; therefore, the fruit has now been realized exactly as previously vowed.

The light of the Dharma-body is immeasurable because it extends vertically through all time and pervades horizontally across all space; the light of the Reward-body is immeasurable because it accords with the true nature of reality (dharmatā); thus, the Way of every Buddha is the same.

As for the radiance of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), there are those that illuminate one yojana, or ten, a hundred, or a thousand yojanas; some illuminate a single world-system, while others illuminate ten, a hundred, or a thousand world-systems. Only Amitābha’s light universally illuminates the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; therefore, he is specifically named "Immeasurable Light" (Amitābha).
However, the three bodies are neither identical nor different; they are merely distinguished in this way for the sake of enabling sentient beings to obtain the four benefits.
Second, the explanation based on lifespan, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the explicit clarification that the lifespans of both the principal and the associates are immeasurable.
2. Furthermore, it indicates that he has already completed ten kalpas since attaining enlightenment.
First: "Moreover, Śāriputra!"
"The lifespan of that Buddha and his people lasts for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, he is named Amitābha.

This is equivalent to saying that the lifespans of both that Buddha and his people are all immeasurable, boundless, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas; this is because in the Western Regions (India), inverted phrasing is frequently employed.

Because the nature of the mind is luminous yet eternally quiescent, it constitutes life-span; now, having thoroughly realized the immeasurable essence of the nature of the mind, one’s life-span is immeasurable.
The life-span of the Dharma-body is immeasurable because it is without beginning and without end; the life-span of the Reward-body is immeasurable because it has a beginning but no end.
This, too, is the common path of all Buddhas, and all may be named Amitāyus (Infinite Life).
As for the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), its duration is extended or shortened according to vows and according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Now, because the Bhikṣu Dharmākara previously made forty-eight vows—including the vow that the Buddha’s own lifespan and the lifespans of the people would both be infinite—the fruit of his attainment now accords with those prior vows; thus, he is specifically named Amitāyus.
This [number] is actually finite; it is merely called "immeasurable" because humans and devas cannot count it.
However, since the three bodies are neither identical nor different, the response body (nirmāṇakāya) may likewise be the immeasurability of the immeasurable.
Question:
"It may be that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable; however, how can the lifespans of the people also be immeasurable? Answer:

"Because the power of the Buddha’s original vow is inconceivable, and because the merit of upholding the Name through faith and aspiration is inconceivable; thus, faith, aspiration, and the upholding of the Name constitute the direct causes and conditions, while the power of the Buddha’s original vow constitutes the dominant condition."
2. Furthermore, it indicates that ten kalpas have already passed since his attainment of Buddhahood:
"Śāriputra, from the time Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood until now, ten kalpas have elapsed."

Since the preceding passage has already clarified that Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma, and this passage further clarifies that his future lifespan is immeasurable, it now further clarifies that he attained Buddhahood in the past ten kalpas ago.
However, the Dharmakāya is fundamentally neither accomplished nor unaccomplished, and thus should not be discussed in terms of kalpas;

the Sambhogakāya is called "accomplished" when its causes are perfected and its fruits are fulfilled, while the Nirmāṇakāya is called "accomplished" when it manifests birth for the sake of sentient beings—both of these may be discussed in terms of kalpas.

Furthermore, since the Dharma-body is manifested through the cultivation of merit, it may be discussed in terms of its accomplishment and its kalpas; the Reward-body has nothing newly acquired and thus lacks such distinctions; and the Response-body, like the moon reflected in a river, neither comes into being nor ceases to be, and likewise should not be discussed in terms of kalpas.

However, each Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment has its own fundamental reality (*honji*) and its manifested traces (*sujaku*); the fundamental realities are all unfathomable. For now, taking the manifested trace of attaining enlightenment shown in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss as an example, it has been ten *kalpas* since he became a Buddha. This is the principle that the three bodies (*trikāya*) are attained as one, where the attainment of one is the attainment of all; it is an attainment discussed in terms of being neither attained nor unattained.
Question:
"The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
'The past and the future are both not substantially existent.'"
"Now, why can it be said that ten kalpas have passed in the past and there are immeasurable [kalpas] in the future? Answer:
"The past and the future are neither manifest nor permanent; therefore, they cannot be grasped as truly existent, yet how could they be grasped as definitely non-existent?"

Furthermore, regarding phenomena of a single present moment, even if one were to grant that they possess substantial entity and function within the Vijñaptimātra system, does it not state that they perish immediately without interval and cannot endure for even a brief moment? How, then, could such things ever be held to be definitively real or definitively permanent?

One must understand that because it is spoken in relation to the present, the past is said to comprise ten kalpas; yet since the past has already ceased, how could there be another ten kalpas accumulated elsewhere that have not yet dissolved?

Furthermore, because it refers to the present, it speaks of future life-span as being immeasurable; yet since the future has not yet arrived, how could there be separate immeasurable kalpas already stored somewhere that gradually arrive?

One must know that time and kalpas have no inherent nature; therefore, the three periods of time are, in their very essence, entirely empty. Yet, this lack of inherent nature is not a state of annihilation, so the distinctions between time and kalpas remain vividly present. Although these distinctions appear vividly, they are all merely reflections manifested within a single present kṣaṇa.
Therefore it is said:
"Throughout ten generations of past and present, from beginning to end, nothing departs from the present moment of thought.
Reflect upon this!
First, the excellence of the Teacher is clarified.
Second, the excellence of the retinue is clarified, which is further divided into two:
first, the excellence of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; [the second follows].
2. The Excellence of Non-retrogression for Those Born [in the Pure Land].
Now, for the first [part]: "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats, beyond what can be known through calculation;
the assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise so.
"Śāriputra! That buddha-land is adorned with such accomplished merits. Question:
The *Treatise on Rebirth* states:
"Those of the two vehicles are not born [there].
Why, then, does that Buddha still have śrāvaka disciples?"
Answer: "Those of the two vehicles with fixed natures who do not dedicate themselves toward bodhi nor make great vows cannot be born there;
however, if those who previously practiced the lesser vehicle turn their merit toward bodhi and make such vows at the time of death, they will indeed be able to be born there."

Although they have attained birth [in this realm], because their previous practice was slight while their past karma was mature, the Buddha accords with their capacities and teaches them the Dharma of the Small Vehicle; they then quickly realize the fruit and immediately turn toward the Great Vehicle, never remaining stuck in the Small Vehicle to the end.

Therefore, these are not the śrāvakas of the Tripitaka Teaching in this land, who must wait until the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* brings about the opening and merging [of the teachings] before they can enter the Perfect [Teaching]. They must be śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching, or perhaps those of the Distinct Teaching who have already severed the afflictions of views and thought at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), and are thus called "Arhats."

Generally, the two teachings [of the Tripitaka and Shared] do not involve hearing the names of Buddhas in other directions; since one has now heard the name of Amitābha and, through faith and aspiration, seeks rebirth there, this is entirely subsumed within the Distinct and Complete Teachings.

The śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are beyond calculation; they are all the result of Amitābha’s great vows and great practices during his causal stage. Therefore, it is said that he has "accomplished such adornments of merit."
2. Second, those who are born there do not regress from the sublime state.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all those born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are non-retrogressive (avaivartika). Among them, there are many who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha); their number is so vast that it cannot be known by calculation, but can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya)."
"Avaivartika" (阿鞞跋致) is translated here as "non-retrogression," and it possesses three meanings:
first, non-retrogression in stage (*avasthā-avaivartika*), because having entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*), one does not fall back to the level of ordinary beings;
second, non-retrogression in practice (*caryā-avaivartika*), because one constantly desires to deliver sentient beings and does not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Third, non-retrogression in mindfulness (*smṛti-avaivartika*), because mind-moment after mind-moment one flows into *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

If categorized according to this land [of Jambudvīpa]: the first fruit of the *āgama* (Śrāvaka), the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) of the *abhijñā* (Pratyekabuddha), the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), and the first level of faith of the Perfect Teaching (*samyak-yāna*) are called non-retrogression in rank; the general Bodhisattva stages, the ten practices (*caryā*) of the Distinct Teaching, and the ten levels of faith of the Perfect Teaching are called non-retrogression in practice; and the first ground (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching are called non-retrogression in mindfulness.

Now, within the Pure Land, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds may, through the fulfillment of ten recitations, attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens; though they rank in the lowest of the lower grades, they all, as a rule, attain the three non-regressions, because the Pure Land lacks any conditions for regression.

Furthermore, once born in the Pure Land, their lifespans will all be immeasurable; they will progress spontaneously through cultivation until reaching the stage of "one-life-to-enlightenment" (ekajātipratibaddha). Observing which of the worlds in the ten directions are devoid of Buddhas or where sentient beings' faculties have ripened, they will immediately go there to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood.
Therefore, those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) are so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation.
First, the detailed exposition of the wondrous fruits of the environment and its inhabitants in that land, intended to inspire faith, is concluded.
II. Properly Exhorting Sentient Beings to Make Vows and Recite the Name to Form the Cause, in three parts:
First, exhorting them to make vows;
second, exhorting them to establish practice.
III. Summary and Exhortation. First: “Śāriputra!...”
Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow to be reborn in that land.
Why is this? Because they will be able to dwell together in one place with such superior and virtuous people.

Having previously exhorted deep faith by citing the wondrous fruits of the environment and inhabitants of that land, he now further exhorts those who hear and believe to make vows accordingly to seek rebirth there; these two—faith and the vow—are the essential keys to rebirth in the Pure Land.

Why is this? If one has not heard the names of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and its environment and inhabitants, or if one hears them explained yet refuses to believe, then it cannot be called "hearing."
Now that you have heard this, you belong to the initial stage of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings; therefore, I instruct you to resolve to attain Bodhi.

Although that land encompasses all four realms of existence, it lies beyond the triple world of this Sahā world and is not the realm of the partial emptiness of the *parinirvāṇa* realized by those of the Two Vehicles. Thus, if one is willing to resolve to seek rebirth there, one is immediately encompassed by the great vows of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. Since one seeks neither the blessings and rewards of humans and devas nor the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, what is this if not the Great Vow for Bodhi!
If one were to seek rebirth in the realms of humans or devas, or to pursue the state of quiescence, that would not constitute the vow to be born in that land.

Therefore, this vow to be born in that land arises from deep faith; when this faith and vow are unified, they serve as the guide for the Pure Land, while the subsequent practice of upholding the Name constitutes the primary cultivation.
If one’s faith and aspiration are firm and steadfast, even ten recitations or a single recitation at the moment of death will certainly result in rebirth.

Conversely, if one lacks faith and aspiration, even if one takes this Name as a meditative focus and maintains it until it becomes like a silver wall or iron fortress—impervious to the wind and undrenched by the rain—it is impossible for even one in ten thousand to attain rebirth in the Pure Land; those who practice the path of Pure Land must not fail to understand this.
The passage beginning with "Why is this so? serves to raise a question and provide an explanation for the necessity of making a vow to be reborn there.

The phrase "to be able to assemble in one place with such superior virtuous people" refers to the countless *arhats*, countless bodhisattvas, and even countless beings in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) mentioned in the preceding text.
If one lacks great faith and great vows, how could one possibly meet with these various superior and virtuous people in one place?
The *Amitābha Sūtra* (Dàběn Āmítuó Jīng) also takes the aspiration for Bodhicitta as its essential point; it is precisely the same as this.
2. Exhortation to Practice:
"Śāriputra, one cannot be born in that land by means of few roots of goodness, merit, or causal conditions."

Śāriputra! If there are good men or good women who hear the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name—whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days—with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, together with a multitude of holy beings, will appear before them. At the end of their life, their minds will not be inverted, and they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

Those born in the Pure Land immediately attain non-retrogression and dwell together in one place with all the most virtuous beings; since this is such an inconceivable dharma-gate of horizontal transcendence, it cannot be attained by those whose roots of goodness and merit are meager.
The correct path to enlightenment is called the "roots of goodness" (kuśalamūla), which constitutes the direct cause;
various factors that assist the path, such as giving, ethical discipline, and meditation, are called "merit" (puṇya), which constitute the auxiliary conditions.

The names "śrāvaka," "pratyekabuddha," and "bodhi" refer to minor roots of goodness; the tainted meritorious karma of humans and devas refers to minor merit. None of these can lead one to birth in the Pure Land. Only by upholding the Name through faith and aspiration does every single sound thereof come to encompass manifold roots of goodness and merit. Even if one calls the Name with a distracted mind, the roots of goodness and merit remain immeasurable—how much more so when the mind is undistracted!

Thus, the Way of resonance and response intermingles, such that the written characters dissolve like a broken seal; the holy assembly of Amitābha does not come, yet comes to personally receive and guide the practitioner, while the practitioner’s consciousness does not go, yet goes to take up a physical form upon a precious lotus.

"Good sons and good daughters"—this term does not distinguish between the laity and the ordained, nor does it consider noble or humble, old or young; furthermore, it places no restriction on those within the six destinies or four modes of birth. Anyone who hears the name of the Buddha has, in fact, matured their roots of goodness over many kalpas; even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil acts are then called good sons and good daughters.
Hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha is the wisdom of hearing; upholding His name is the wisdom of reflection; and single-mindedness without distraction is the wisdom of cultivation.

Amitābha Buddha is the great name encompassing all virtues; by invoking virtue through this name, nothing is left unexhausted. Therefore, upholding the name is taken as the primary practice, without the necessity of further engaging in practices such as visualization or investigative inquiry. It is thus most simple and most direct.

To hear and believe, and having believed to form a vow, one is then willing to uphold [the name]; those who do not believe, do not vow, or have not heard are equal [to those who have not heard]. Although these may still serve as remote causes, they are not called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Upholding [the name], however, involves recollecting the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment, and is therefore "wisdom derived from reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
However, there is both the maintenance through phenomena (*dharma*) and the maintenance through principle (*tattva*).

As for maintenance through phenomena: one believes that Amitābha Buddha exists in the Western Quarter, yet has not yet realized that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha. Because one merely resolves with a firm vow to seek birth [in that land], constantly and without momentary forgetfulness—like a child yearning for its mother—it is called maintenance through phenomena.

Regarding "holding by principle": one believes that Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter is fully possessed within one's own mind and created by one's own mind. One then takes this great name—possessed and created by one's own mind—as the object for binding the mind, ensuring it is not forgotten for even a moment; this is called "holding by principle."
"From one day up to seven days" refers to fixing a specific period to accomplish the task.

Those of sharp faculties attain non-distraction in a single day; those of dull faculties only attain non-distraction after seven days; and for those of middling faculties, it is indefinite, occurring on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day.

Furthermore, those of sharp faculties can remain undisturbed for seven days; those of dull faculties can barely remain undisturbed for one day; and those of middling faculties remain undisturbed for six, five, four, three, or two days, as it is not fixed.
To maintain this until one reaches the state of "single-mindedness without distraction" constitutes the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
There are two types of single-mindedness:

whether it be maintaining through phenomena (*dharma*) or maintaining through principle (*li*), as long as one maintains the practice until the afflictions (*kleśa*) are suppressed and eliminated, and even the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are first exhausted, all such instances are termed "phenomenal single-mindedness."

Furthermore, whether one maintains the practice through phenomena (*dharma*) or through principle (*li*), maintaining it until the sincere mind opens and reveals the Buddha of the original nature is all termed "principle single-mindedness" (*li yixin*).
Phenomenal single-mindedness is not disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while principle single-mindedness is not disturbed by the two extremes (*antadvaya*).

Because one is not disturbed by the afflictions of views and thoughts, the transformation-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) and the assembly of sages appear before them. Their minds no longer give rise to the inverted perceptions of the three realms of existence within the Sahā world; they immediately attain rebirth in the two types of Sukhāvatī worlds: the Land of Common Dwelling and the Land of Skillful Means.

Being undisturbed by the two extremes, the Sambhogakāya Buddha and the assembly of sages appear before them; their minds no longer give rise to the inverted views of the duality of birth-and-death and nirvana, and they immediately attain rebirth in the two types of Ultimate Bliss worlds: the Realm of True Reward and the Realm of Quiescent Light.

One should know that although holding the name is simple and direct, it is nevertheless sudden and perfect. Because a single thought in accord with reality is itself a Buddha-thought, and every thought in accord with reality is itself a Buddha-thought, there is no need for arduous visualization nor the necessity of investigative inquiry; it is immediately perfectly luminous, without remainder or deficiency. Those of the highest faculties can never surpass its threshold, yet even those of the lowest faculties may reach its gate. It may be said to span horizontally across the Eight Teachings and penetrate vertically through the Five Periods; thus, out of ultimate compassion, the Buddha spoke of it spontaneously without being asked, and deeply lamented its difficulty of belief.
Question:
"When a Buddha appears at the moment of death, how can one be certain it is not a demon? Answer:

"For one who cultivates the mind, the Buddha suddenly appears even without practicing the contemplation of the Buddha; since this was not originally expected, it is called a demonic affair (*māra-karman*).

However, if seeing the Buddha through mindfulness of the Buddha is already a state of resonance (*saṃprayoga*), how much more so when it occurs at the time of death, which is no longer a time for demons to cause trouble! Why, then, should there be any doubt?"
Question: "Does 'not being disturbed for seven days' refer to ordinary times,
or does it refer to the time of death?"
Answer: “It refers to ordinary times. Question:
"If we consider ordinary circumstances, suppose there were a person who, after seven days of non-confusion, again gives rise to delusion and creates karma; would they still be reborn?"
Answer: "If one truly attains a state of single-mindedness without distraction, there will certainly never again be the occurrence of giving rise to delusions or creating karma. Question:
"Regarding the 'ten recitations of the Great Sutra' and the 'single recitation of the Treasure King,' does this refer to ordinary times or to the time of death? Answer:

"The ten recitations apply to both occasions: if they are the ten recitations performed at dawn, they belong to the period of ordinary practice; if the ten recitations result in rebirth, they are identical to the ten vocal invocations in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, though that refers specifically to the time of approaching death. As for the single recitation, it refers exclusively to the moment of death."
Question: "Since both ten recitations and a single recitation can lead to rebirth, why does this sutra require seven days? Answer:
"If one lacks the seven days of practice during one's ordinary life, how can there be even ten recitations or a single recitation at the moment of death?

Even those described in the *Amitābha Sūtra* as being reborn in the lowest of the lower grades—people who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds and have never practiced in this present life—all do so because their past causes have matured; thus they encounter virtuous friends at the end of life and, upon hearing [the teaching], immediately develop faith and aspiration. Such occurrences happen but once in ten thousand cases. How could one fail to prepare the provisions in advance and instead rely on a mere chance among ten thousand?"
Question: "The Western Land is one hundred trillion worlds away from here; how can one be reborn there so immediately? Answer:

"The hundred trillion lands do not lie outside the single thought-moment of my present mind-nature, for the mind-nature is fundamentally without exterior; furthermore, by relying on the Buddha’s power to receive and guide me, how could it be difficult to be born there immediately?"

Question: "Since it has been determined that faith and aspiration belong to the practice of wisdom (prajñā-caryā) and the holding of the name belongs to the practice of conduct (caryā-caryā), then the recitation and upholding of the Name should be considered an auxiliary practice; why is it called the primary practice?"
"How can each and every sound fully possess manifold roots of goodness and merit?
Answer: "It is based on the teaching of faith, aspiration, and practice within a single mind; they do not have a sequence of before and after, nor are they fixed as three."

Indeed, without aspiration and practice, it cannot be called true faith; without practice and faith, it cannot be called true aspiration; and without faith and aspiration, it cannot be called true practice. Now, since one holds the Name entirely through faith and aspiration, each and every utterance fully embodies all three—faith, aspiration, and practice. This is why it is said to be the cause and condition for manifold roots of goodness and merit.
This refers to what is stated in the *Amitābha Sūtra*: "Because one invokes the name of the Buddha, in every thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated.
If one’s roots of goodness and merit were not extensive, how could such great sins as these be eliminated?

Question: "Because the power of mindfulness at the moment of death is so intense and urgent, it can eliminate the sins of many kalpas; if one recites the name with a sincere mind during ordinary times, will that also eliminate sin? Answer:
"Just as the rising sun naturally dispels the masses of darkness, so too do all myriad transgressions naturally perish when one invokes the great name of the Buddha.
Question: "Can one who invokes the name with a distracted mind also eliminate their transgressions and attain rebirth?"
Answer: "One must also eliminate transgressions; rebirth is not guaranteed.
That one must eliminate transgressions is because the merit of the Name is truly inconceivable."
Rebirth is not guaranteed, for the indeterminate and scattered roots of goodness are difficult to counteract the heavy sins accumulated since beginningless time.

This is truly because the heavy sins of birth and death committed by us throughout kalpas since the beginningless past—if these heavy sins possessed a physical form or characteristics—could not be contained even within the entirety of the realm of empty space. Thus, although one may recite the name of Amitābha a hundred thousand times every single day and night throughout a hundred years from birth until death, thereby extinguishing eighty billion kalpas of heavy sins of birth and death with each utterance, the sins thus extinguished are like the dirt under a fingernail, while the sins not yet extinguished are like the soil of the great earth. Only when one can maintain mindfulness until reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction" will one be like a strong man breaking through an encirclement, no longer subject to the control of the three armies!
Question: "Since rebirth is not fixed, what benefit is there in reciting the name? Answer:
"A single recitation of the Buddha's name constitutes the seed for attaining Buddhahood; it is like a vajra, ultimately indestructible.

Thus, in the time of the Buddha, there was an old man who wished to leave the household life. Five hundred noble disciples observed him with their eyes of the Path and all concluded that he lacked the roots of goodness, refusing to grant him ordination."
Later, he went to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha immediately ordained him.
The disciples asked the Buddha about the causes and conditions for this, and the Buddha said:

"In immeasurable kalpas past, this man entered the mountains to gather firewood and was pursued by a tiger. He climbed a tree to escape it, but the tiger continued to circle the tree, pawing and roaring. Because of his extreme terror, he lost his voice and involuntarily cried out, 'Namo Buddha'."
"Now these roots of goodness have matured, and having encountered me, they have attained the Way; this is not something that can be known by the Dharma-eye of the followers of the two vehicles.

Judging from this, what is clarified in the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is that if, in the presence of past Buddhas, one has even casually invoked the Buddha's name, all have already attained Buddhahood.
Is this not truly credible!

I humbly pray that whether you be monastics or laypeople, wise or ignorant, regarding this simple, direct, and unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the Perfect and Sudden, do not regard it as difficult and thus give rise to retreat or procrastination; do not regard it as easy and thus neglect to exert yourselves; do not regard it as shallow and thus treat it with contemptuous disdain; and do not regard it as profound and thus feel daunted by the responsibility of undertaking it.

The names and titles that are upheld are truly inconceivable, and the nature of the mind that upholds them is likewise truly inconceivable. To uphold one name is for that one name to be inconceivable; to uphold ten names, a hundred names, or even immeasurable and innumerable names, it is because every single name is entirely inconceivable.
2. Summary and Exhortation:
"Śāriputra, it is because I see this benefit that I have spoken these words."
"If there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land.

What the Buddha’s eye perceives is exhaustive and perfectly clear: to uphold the Name with faith and vow is indeed a matter of many roots of goodness and merit; by virtue of these roots of goodness and merit, one will certainly be welcomed by the Buddha and the assembly of sages, and will certainly be born in the four types of Pure Lands of Ultimate Bliss—this is the benefit of inconceivable merit.
Therefore, he earnestly exhorts us again to resolve to be reborn [in the Pure Land], for aspiration can guide practice.
Part Two, the Main Body (Zhengzongfen), concludes.
Part Three, the Dissemination Section (Liutongfen): the three factors of faith, aspiration, and practice fully encompass the essential purport of this entire sutra.

Since this unsurpassed Dharma-gate is profoundly deep and difficult to believe, the Buddha, having no one to question him, spoke of his own accord to initiate the discourse; he further cited the broad and long tongues of the Buddhas of the six directions as witnesses to ensure its widespread circulation.

Were it not for the power of circulation, how could the wondrous Dharma—this raft and trap—be prevented from being obstructed in future ages, and how could these essential points of the Perfect and Sudden teaching be transmitted eternally to those who have not yet heard them?
The text is divided into five sections:
first, citing the praise and exhortation for circulation by the Buddhas of the six directions to encourage faith and dissemination;
second, re-examining the title and providing an explanation to encourage faith and dissemination.
Third, exhorting the circulation [of the teaching] by way of those who have already been born, those currently being born, and those yet to be born;
fourth, strengthening faith in the circulation through citing the praise of all Buddhas for this difficult task;
fifth, the joyful reception and acceptance of the circulation by the great assembly.
The first section contains six items:
first, the eastern direction, up to sixth, the upper direction.
Although the Tang translation speaks of the "ten directions," one should know that while the text varies in detail, there is no difference in meaning.
Now, first: "Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable benefits of the meritorious virtues of Amitābha Buddha."

In the eastern direction, there are also Buddhas such as Akṣobhya, Merudhvaja, Mahāmeru, Meruprabhāsa, and Gadgadasvara—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Each, in his own land, extends his broad and long tongue, covering the entire trichiliocosm, and speaks these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."

Continuing from the preceding section on the Main Body of the Teaching, which extensively praises the adornments of the environment and the beings of Amitābha Buddha and exhorts people to attain the stage of non-retrogression directly through faith, aspiration, and the recitation of His name—this is particularly inconceivable among all worldly and supramundane merits and benefits. Therefore, it is not only Śākyamuni Tathāgata who offers praise; indeed, all the Buddhas of the six directions, without exception, praise this with one voice and in harmony.
Regarding the term "inconceivable," there are briefly five meanings:
first, it involves transcending the three realms horizontally without waiting for the gradual severance of afflictions;
second, it involves the horizontal presence of the four lands within the Western Pure Land itself, rather than through gradual realization.
Third, because one merely upholds the name without relying on meditative contemplation or other skillful means;
fourth, because one takes seven days as the period without depending on many kalpas, many lifetimes, or many years and months;
fifth, because upholding the name of a single Buddha constitutes being protected and remembered by all Buddhas, no differently than upholding the names of all Buddhas.
"Akṣobhya" is translated here as "Immovable"; the others may all be understood accordingly.

The Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues and thus must have immeasurable names. These names are established according to the capacities of sentient beings; they may be derived from causes or effects, from nature or characteristics, or from practices and vows. Although these represent only a partial illustration of one aspect, each nonetheless embodies the four *siddhāntas*. Each individual name reveals the virtues it signifies, such that even if one were to speak of them for an entire eon, they could never be exhausted; they can only be comprehended through the mind’s understanding.
Because the space of the eastern direction is inexhaustible, the worlds therein are also inexhaustible.

Because the worlds are inexhaustible, the Buddhas currently dwelling in those worlds are likewise inexhaustible; I shall briefly cite five names to represent all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Thus, each of these Buddhas extends their broad and long tongues to speak words of truth, exhorting all to believe in this sutra; yet sentient beings still fail to produce faith—their stubborn ignorance is extreme indeed.
Regarding the mark of the broad and long tongue: an ordinary person who has not spoken falsely throughout the three periods of time can extend their tongue to touch their nose;

however, because the Buddha, the one who attained the fruit of the hidden head, did not speak falsely for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, his tongue is thin, broad, and long, such that it can emerge and cover his face.
Now, having realized the wondrous gateway to the Pure Land of the Mahāyāna, it pervades the trichiliocosm to manifest that these words are necessarily sincere and by no means false or erroneous.

The formal title of this sutra is "The Sutra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas. Because Master Kumārajīva translated it as simply "The Buddha-spoken Amitābha Sutra" to accord with the local preference for brevity, and because Master Xuánzàng adopted a middle path between the two, translating it as "The Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas' Acceptance," one should know that while these versions differ in the detail of their phrasing, they do not vary in their underlying meaning.
2. The Southern Direction.

“Śāriputra! In the worlds of the southern direction there are Buddhas such as Candrasūryapradīpa, Yaśaḥprabha, Mahārciskandha, Merupradīpa, and Anantavīrya—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Each, in his own land, extends his broad and long tongue until it completely covers the trichiliocosm, and speaks these words of truth:”
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Merits of Praise, which is inconceivable and is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. 3. The West.

“Śāriputra! In the western world-system there are Buddhas such as Amitāyus, Amitābha, Amitadhvaja, Mahāprabha, Mahārciskandha, Ratnākara, and Śuddharaśmiprabha—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Each, in his own land, extends his broad and long tongue until it completely covers the trichiliocosm, and speaks these truthful words:
‘You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra which praises inconceivable merit and is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.’”
Question: "Is Amitāyus Buddha the same as Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Answer:
"It is both 'it is so' and 'it is not so. Regarding 'it is so':
the Buddha has no mark of self; yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he does not refrain from praising himself, just as Śākyamuni also praised himself."
"It is not that [the name] may also be [shared], for the Buddhas in the ten directions who share this same name are immeasurable; it is not merely one Buddha who is named Immeasurable Life.
4. The Northern Direction.

“Śāriputra! In the worlds of the northern direction, there are Buddhas such as Flame-Shoulder Buddha, Most Supreme Sound Buddha, Invincible Buddha, Sun-Born Buddha, and Net-Luminosity Buddha—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Each, in his own land, extends his broad and long tongue until it completely covers the trichiliocosm, and speaks these words of truth:
‘You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Merits of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.’”
5. The Lower Direction. "Śāriputra!

In the worlds of the lower direction, there are Buddhas such as Siṃhanāda Buddha, Yaśas Buddha, Yaśaskīrti Buddha, Dharmaprabhāsa Buddha, Dharmadhvaja Buddha, and Dharmadhara Buddha—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Each, in his own land, extends his broad and long tongue, covering the entire trichiliocosm, and speaks these words of truth:..."
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this Sutra on the Inconceivable Merit of Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.

As for "the lower realms," beneath this world’s water-circle, gold-circle, and wind-circle, there are further lower realms such as the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception, extending through countless, inexhaustible, unspeakable upon unspeakable layers.
*Dharma* is translated here as "Dharma"; the rest may be understood accordingly.
Sixth, the Upper Direction: "Śāriputra!..."

In the worlds above, there are Buddhas such as Brahma-voice Buddha, Constellation King Buddha, Fragrance Supreme Buddha, Fragrant Light Buddha, Great Flame Shoulder Buddha, Adorned Body with Variegated Jewel Flower Buddha, Śāla Tree King Buddha, Jewel Flower Virtue Buddha, Seeing All Meanings Buddha, and Tathāgata Like Mount Sumeru Buddha. These and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each from their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues until they completely cover the trichiliocosm, and speak these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sūtra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas."

Regarding "the regions above": beyond this realm and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), there are further upper realms consisting of wind-wheels, silver-wheels, the three realms, and so forth—repeatedly layered and inexhaustible, beyond all description, even beyond the ineffable.
Question:
"Since there are Buddhas in each of the six directions, there must also necessarily be pure lands for each; why then do you single out the western direction for praise? Answer:

"This is because it allows beginners to easily set their minds upon the goal; furthermore, because Amitābha’s original vows are supreme; furthermore, because sentient beings of this land have a particularly strong affinity with him; and furthermore, because recollecting a single Buddha, Amitābha, constitutes recollecting immeasurable Buddhas, and being born in a single pure land, the Western Paradise, constitutes being born in all immeasurable pure lands."
If those at a shallow stage of practice know that the Western Quarter is superior to other directions, they may resolutely set their minds on seeking it exclusively;

if those at a profound stage of practice know that the Western Quarter subsumes the ten directions and encompasses the four lands, they need not abandon the West to seek elsewhere for the Flower Treasury World (Huazang).

If one were to claim that the Western Paradise is provisional while the Flower Treasury World is ultimate, or that the Western Paradise is small while the Flower Treasury World is great, one would fall entirely into the pervasive conceptual attachments of sentient beings; this is because such a person fails to realize that the provisional and the ultimate are of one essence, and that both the small and the great are devoid of intrinsic nature.
First, the section on citing the praise and encouragement for circulation by the Buddhas of the six directions is concluded.
Second, the section on restating the title, providing an explanation, and encouraging belief and circulation: "Śāriputra!..."
"What do you think?
For what reason is it called 'The Sutra Protected by the Recollection of All Buddhas'? Śāriputra!"

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sutra and receive and uphold it, as well as those who hear the names of the various Buddhas, all these good sons and good daughters shall be protected and sustained by all the Buddhas, and they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, you all should believe and accept my words as well as those spoken by all the Buddhas.
*Anuttara* here means "unsurpassed," and *samyaksambodhi* here means "right, complete, and perfect enlightenment," which is the realization of the fruit of the Mahāyāna.

This Mahāyāna sūtra uniquely elucidates the essential core of the mind—simple, direct, perfect, and sudden; furthermore, the names of all Buddhas collectively signify the unsurpassed, perfect, and ultimate myriad virtues. Therefore, those who hear and uphold this sūtra, as well as those who hear the names of the Buddhas, are all protected and remembered by the Buddhas, and all shall attain non-retrogression from Great Bodhi.
Question:

"It may be that one can attain non-retrogression through hearing, upholding, and mindfully recollecting the sutras; but by merely hearing the name of the Buddha, can one also attain non-retrogression through mindful recollection? Answer:
"This meaning has both a restricted and a universal application.
As for the restricted application, the *Sūtra of the Divination of the Ground* states:

'If one possesses a distracted and defiled mind, even though they recite my name, it does not constitute "hearing" [the Dharma]. Because they cannot give rise to resolute faith and understanding, they merely obtain worldly rewards of merit, but do not attain vast, profound, and wondrous benefits.'"

If one attains the Samādhi of One Practice, one then accomplishes a vast and subtle mind of practice; this is called attaining the semblance of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, and it constitutes having heard the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

This case should also be understood in the same way; therefore, one must first hear this sutra and then receive and uphold the method for grasping and maintaining the names of the Buddhas as shown therein. Only by maintaining these names until the mind is single-minded and undisturbed does one come to hear the names of all Buddhas and become protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.

As for what is called "pervasive," the compassion of all Buddhas is inconceivable, and their names and merits are likewise inconceivable; therefore, upon hearing a Buddha's name even once, whether one has a virtuous mind or not, and whether one believes or slanders, it all becomes a causal seed.

It is like entering a sandalwood forest: whether one bows down or strikes it, one is permeated by its fragrance. How much more so for the Buddha, who delivers sentient beings without discriminating between enemies and kin, never tiring; if one hears the Buddha’s name, the Buddha will surely protect and mind them—so why should there be any doubt?
However, according to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, all three treatises state that only Bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature are protected and remembered by the Buddha;

according to their respective stages, they must be at the level of the Separate Stages (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*) or the Perfect Abiding (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*). This is because it refers solely to those who rely on their own power; therefore, one must enter the nature of co-arising (*sahaja-gotra*) before being eligible for such protection and mindfulness.
Now, by relying on the power of others, one receives protective mindfulness even at the stage of semblance, thereby being able to perfectly attain the three kinds of non-retrogression.

Even down to the single hearing of a Buddha’s name, there is the power of stimulation within the dharma-nature of same essence; thus, one also attains the distant cause that ensures ultimate non-retrogression.
"Since the merit of hearing this name is so great, how could one not believe what has been proclaimed by Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the six directions?
Third, the exhortation for its circulation, based on what has already occurred and what shall yet come to pass.

“Śāriputra! If there are people who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow, desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, all such persons shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Whether they have already been born, are now being born, or will be born in that land, they shall all abide in non-retrogression.”
Therefore, Śāriputra, if there are good sons and good daughters who possess faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land.

Those who have already made the vow are those who have already been born; those who are making the vow now are those being born now; and those who will make the vow in the future are those who will be born in the future. This clearly demonstrates that the vow made in reliance upon faith is never made in vain, but will certainly bear fruit.
Without faith, one cannot form a vow; yet even with faith, if one does not form a vow, [the aspiration] will not arise. Therefore, he earnestly exhorts us again to form a vow.
A vow is the warrant for faith and the pivot of practice; it is a matter of supreme importance. When the vow is undertaken, faith and practice are contained within it.
Question:
"One who makes a vow now should only be able to attain it in a future life; how can you say 'if in this life'? Answer:

"This also has two meanings: First, 'now' is used generally to refer to a single lifetime; thus, if one makes vows and recites the Name in the present life, one will certainly attain birth in the Pure Land at the end of life. This 'making vows now' refers precisely to the present life. Second, 'now' is used specifically to refer to a single moment (kṣaṇa);

thus, with one thought-moment of resonance, there is birth in one thought-moment, and with every thought-moment of resonance, there is birth in every thought-moment. The wondrous cause and wondrous fruit are not separate from the one mind, like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a scale. Why wait until the retribution of the Sahā world is exhausted before being nurtured in the Jewel Pond?"
Now, by means of faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name, one is no longer a person within the Sahā world.
This is most perfect and most sudden, difficult to discuss and difficult to conceive; only those with great wisdom can truly believe it.
4. Citing the praise of all Buddhas for difficult tasks to encourage faith and ensure circulation.
This section also has two parts; first:
First, citing the Buddhas to praise it in concert;
second, personally concluding with a lament over its difficulty to believe.
Now, the first [point].

“Śāriputra! Just as I now praise the inconceivable merit of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas praise my own inconceivable merit, saying: ‘The Buddha Śākyamuni is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat;

he has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi within the Sahā world-system, amidst the five corruptions of this evil age—the corruption of the kalpa, the corruption of views, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of sentient beings, and the corruption of lifespan—and for the sake of all sentient beings, he preaches this Dharma that is difficult for the entire world to believe.’”
Although the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas are equal, their methods of transformation differ in terms of ease and difficulty.
It is easy to attain enlightenment in a pure land, but difficult to attain enlightenment in a defiled world;
it is easy to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in a pure land, but difficult to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in a defiled world.
To preach the gradual Dharma for sentient beings in this defiled age is still relatively easy; to preach the sudden Dharma is even more difficult.
To preach other sudden teachings for sentient beings in this defiled age is still relatively easy; to preach this sudden method of horizontal transcendence in the Pure Land is even more difficult.

To preach the wondrous contemplation of sudden cultivation and sudden realization through the horizontal transcendence of the Pure Land for sentient beings in this defiled age is already no small matter; yet to preach this supreme, wondrous, and inconceivable first expedient—which requires no arduous effort for cultivation or realization, but allows one to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression by merely holding the Name—is the most difficult among all difficulties.
Because these nine dharma-realms of the world are difficult for all to believe, they are called an extremely rare and marvelous matter.
Furthermore, among all the Buddhas of the ten directions, there is not one who does not praise and extol me, Śākyamuni, as being preeminently courageous and valiant.
The *kalpa-kaṣāya* (defilement of the eon) refers to the time when defiled phenomena gather together.

The *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (defilement of views) refers to the flourishing of the five types of speculative views—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various false views—which are called "defilements" because they are dark, obscure, and submerged in delusion.

Regarding the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*): it refers to the flourishing of the five dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt; because they cause agitation and distress, they are called "turbidity."

Regarding the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*): it refers to the false designation of "sentient beings" as a composite of the coarse and inferior five aggregates produced by views and afflictions; because both their physical form and mental faculties are base and deficient, it is called a "defilement."

Regarding the defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*): because both cause and effect are inferior and lifespans are short, such that they do not even reach a full hundred years, it is called a "defilement.
Second, [the author] personally expresses the difficulty of faith.

“Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task by attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and preaching this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the worlds; this is truly most difficult.”

"Faithful recitation of the Name with aspiration ensures that out of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand are liberated; they will forever leave the five turbidities behind and perfectly purify the four lands. Such a wondrous Dharma is truly difficult to believe; therefore, not only do all Buddhas praise it, but I myself also marvel at its extreme difficulty."
Were it not for the great compassion and vast vow that have perfumed the mind through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, how could one perform such a difficult task?
To lack faith in this is to deeply辜负 (betray) the World-Honored One of Compassion.

"When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated themselves, and departed."
This Dharma gate is inconceivable, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand; therefore, not a single person was able to pose a question.
The Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities of beings, and knowing that their faculties were now mature, he spoke of his own accord without being asked, so that they might obtain the four benefits.
Having heard it, they received it with joy and faith, like a timely rain that brings transformation.

"Joy" refers to the serenity and delight of body and mind; "faith" refers to being entirely free from doubt; "receiving" refers to grasping and retaining it without forgetting; "prostrating" refers to feeling great gratitude and bowing down in submission; and "departing" refers to practicing according to the teaching and never retreating.
**Epilogue to the Essential Explanation of the Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra** The Sūtra states:

"In the age of the Dharma’s decay, among billions upon billions of people who practice, it is rare for even one to attain the Way; only by relying on the recitation of the Buddha's name can one obtain deliverance."
"Alas! Now is precisely the time for this! If one abandons this inconceivable Dharma-gate, how could one possibly achieve excellence?

Even at the time of my initial renunciation, I relied on the *Zongcheng* (School of the Lineage) and held myself in high esteem while looking down upon the scriptural teachings, falsely claiming that the practice of reciting the name was merely a provisional method for those of middling or inferior capacity. Later, due to a severe illness, I resolved to return to the West; subsequently, through further study of the *Miaozong* and *Yuanzhong* commentaries, as well as the Yunqi commentaries and other texts, I finally realized that the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is truly the Unsurpassed King of Jewels. Only then did I become willing to apply my whole heart to holding the name, such that ten thousand oxen could not have turned me back."

My friend, the Great Being Dujing, has long devoted himself to the practice of pure karma; wishing to ensure that the essential meaning of this sutra is clearly manifest without excessive verbiage, he charged me with composing this essential commentary.
Since I myself desire to universally cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to be born together in Sukhāvatī, it was logically impossible for me to decline.
I took up my brush on the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of the Dinghai year and completed the transcription on the fifth day of the tenth month; it was accomplished in nine days.

It is my wish that every phrase and every character may serve as a provision for the path, and that all who see or hear this may together reach the stage of non-retrogression. Whether they believe or doubt, may they all plant the seeds of the Way; whether they praise or slander, may they equally attain liberation.
I look up with reverence to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to receive them and bear witness, and to my fellow students and friends for their sympathetic joy and spiritual protection.
The monk Ouyi Zhixu sets down his brush here as a postscript; he was forty-nine years of age at the time.
The postscript to the *Commentary on the Essentials of the Amitābha Sūtra* quotes the Sūtra as saying:
"The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. An ancient said:
Contemplating that the self-nature of Amitābha is born from the pure land of the mind-only—

when these are viewed together, the meaning of "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," such that there is no Buddha outside the mind and no mind outside the Buddha, becomes clear!

Later generations, failing to comprehend this, abandoned the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to speak instead of the "Mind-Only Pure Land," and set aside the World-Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues and Compassion to speak instead of the "Self-Nature Amitābha. Is this not tantamount to asserting that there is a Buddha outside the mind, or a mind outside the Buddha?

Our master Ouyi deeply awakened to the essence of the mind-nature, which is without exterior; thus, whether regarding the schools or the teachings, or the nature or the characteristics, he unified them all under a single principle. Having already composed such works as the *Combined Commentary on the Brahma Net Sutra*, the *Mysterious Text on the Buddha’s Crown*, the *Essentials of Consciousness-Only*, and the *Explanatory Essentials of Mahayana Calm and Contemplation* to elucidate the wondrous principles of the provisional and the real, he further extracted this *Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra* for the sake of those with correct understanding. Upon opening and reading it even once, one feels that those who possess faith, vow, and practice can personally grasp the ticket [to rebirth]; it is truly what is called "direct and incisive, concise in words yet exhaustive in meaning."

In this degenerate age, great masters who propagate the Dharma each specialize in a particular field, and few are able to master both the *Xing* (nature/essence) and the *Xiang* (phenomena/appearance) schools simultaneously. Only Master Ouyi first attained thorough penetration from the source of the mind; thus, regarding the teachings of *Xing*, *Xiang*, the Sutras, and the Treatises, he was as unimpeded as one handling a blade of bamboo. Having realized that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-different in their threefold naturelessness, and that the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are both inherently contained within and constructed by the mind, he understood that all aspects of the Pure Land—both the environment and its inhabitants—are nothing other than manifestations of one's own mind. Consequently, the principles of the four lands in their horizontal and vertical dimensions were as clear to him as pointing at something in the palm of his hand. Nevertheless, this is but a single drop from the ocean of the Dharma!

If you wish to exhaust the depths and boundaries of Master Ouyi’s teachings, you should read widely through his major works, such as the *Hezhù*, the *Xuánwén*, and the *Xīnyào*, and furthermore seek out what lies before the pen is even raised; in this way, you will avoid mistaking the finger for the moon.
